newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: New Yugoslav government has IMF minister.
newsitem.headline: New Yugoslav government has IMF minister.

text.p: Yugoslav Prime Minister Radoje Kontic unveiled a heavily reshuffled government on Thursday including a minister for relations with international financial institutions.
The 21-member socialist-led government included 14 new faces but there were no changes in the foreign, defence and economy ministries.

Kontic named Nobojsa Maljkovic, a banker and member of the small neo-marxist United Yugoslav Left (JUL), as minister in charge of coordinating Yugoslavia's return to membership of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank.
Yugoslavia, comprising Serbia and Montenegro, also wants to join the World Trade Organisation (WTO) and resume membership of international and European diplomatic bodies.

"Regulation of relations with the IMF is of exceptional significance for the Yugoslav economy, since without access to world financial markets and without additional funds we cnnot carry out our ambitious current and future development," Kontic told the federal parliament.
The IMF has postponed further consideration of Yugoslav membership until June at the earliest despite Belgrade's pressing need for access to aid.

Western countries including the United States say Yugoslavia should enact pro-democracy reforms and reach a political accommodation with ethnic Albanians seeking autonomy in the southern province of Kosovo before they will agree to its readmission to the IMF.
Yugoslav membership was suspended under U.N. sanctions imposed to punish Serbs for the role in the Bosnian war.
Lack of access to foreign capital has emerged as the biggest obstacle to rebuilding the economy in the 15 months since sanctions were lifted.
Kontic said the government would also try to reschedule its external debt estimated at around $9 billion.
He had been working on the composition of a new government since the Socialists and their allies won a near two-thirds majority in federal elections last November.

His efforts were delayed by Montenegrin opposition to JUL's attempts to get more than the two ministries it was allocated. JUL leaders include Mirjana Markovic, the unpopular wife of Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic.
Her hardline influence on Milosevic was widely blamed for prolonging a dispute between the socialists and opposition parties over the outcome of municipal elections last November.
Three months of street demonstrations forced Milosevic to accept opposition control of Belgrade and other main cities.
Although JUL's popular support is tiny, its membership includes influential figures among Serbia's business and political elite dating from the communist era.

Despite the need to conciliate the United States over IMF membership, parliament ratified a plan to establish a special relationship between Yugoslavia and the Bosnian Serb republic which Washington said was premature.
